overview:
The Culika-sutras (Cūlikā-sūtras) are a small but significant category within the Śvetāmbara Jain canonical literature. In the traditional classification of the canon, texts are grouped into Aṅgas, Upāṅgas, Cheda-sūtras, Mūla-sūtras, and Cūlikā-sūtras. The Culika-sutras are understood as "supplementary" or "appendant" works that stand in close relation to the Aṅgas, especially in their concern with methods of exposition, hermeneutics, and the framework of scriptural study.

In the Śvetāmbara tradition, two texts are generally counted as Culika-sutras: the Nandi-sūtra and the Anuyogadvāra-sūtra (often written Anuyogadvara-sūtra). Both are composed in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit and are regarded as part of the canonical corpus preserved and transmitted by monastic lineages. They do not primarily present new doctrinal content in the way that some Aṅgas or Upāṅgas do; instead, they systematize and classify the modes of scriptural exposition, the types of questions and arguments, and the categories of knowledge relevant for understanding the broader canon.

The Nandi-sūtra is especially associated with the classification of knowledge (jñāna) and the ways in which omniscience (kevala-jñāna) and scriptural knowledge (śruta-jñāna) are understood. It outlines various kinds of exposition (naya), interpretive approaches, and the relationship between the omniscient perspective and partial viewpoints. In doing so, it provides a conceptual map for how canonical teachings are to be approached and taught, and it is often studied in conjunction with other hermeneutical texts and commentaries.

The Anuyogadvāra-sūtra focuses on the "gateways" (dvāra) to exposition (anuyoga). It classifies different types of scriptural discourse—such as narratives, doctrinal summaries, lists, and analytical discussions—and explains how these forms are used to convey the teachings. The text is important for understanding how Jain teachers historically organized their sermons and scholastic works, and it has influenced later exegetical traditions and scholastic manuals.

Within the broader Jain intellectual history, the Culika-sutras serve as a bridge between the early canonical strata and later systematic philosophy and logic. They provide technical vocabulary and conceptual tools that are taken up by classical Jain philosophers in Sanskrit, such as those writing on epistemology (pramāṇa), viewpoints (naya), and non-one-sidedness (anekāntavāda). At the same time, they retain a strongly practical orientation: they are meant to guide monks, nuns, and advanced students in how to study, memorize, and expound the scriptures responsibly.

Modern scholarship often treats the Culika-sutras as key sources for reconstructing early Jain hermeneutics and pedagogy. Because they are relatively concise and highly structured, they lend themselves to detailed philological and doctrinal analysis. However, their technical nature can make them challenging for beginners, and they are usually studied after one has some familiarity with the basic doctrinal outlines found in other canonical texts. In contemporary Śvetāmbara communities, they continue to be recited, commented upon, and used in advanced scriptural study, especially in monastic education and in specialized lay study circles.

primary_sources.title: Nandi-sūtra (Nandī-sutta)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to the canonical redaction of the Śvetāmbara Jain community; specific individual authorship is not asserted.
primary_sources.original_text: ṇamō arihaṃtāṇaṃ, ṇamō siddhāṇaṃ, ṇamō āyariyāṇaṃ, ṇamō uvajjhāyāṇaṃ, ṇamō loe savva-sāhūṇaṃ.
primary_sources.transliteration: namo arihaṃtāṇaṃ, namo siddhāṇaṃ, namo āyariyāṇaṃ, namo uvajjhāyāṇaṃ, namo loe savva-sāhūṇaṃ.
primary_sources.translation: Homage to the Arhats, homage to the Siddhas, homage to the Ācāryas, homage to the Upādhyāyas, homage to all the Sādhus in the world.
primary_sources.notes: This verse, known widely as the Navakāra or Namaskāra, appears in multiple canonical contexts and is used here as a representative opening formula associated with canonical recitation. The Nandi-sūtra itself proceeds to classify types of knowledge (jñāna), especially scriptural knowledge (śruta-jñāna), and discusses the modes of exposition (naya) and the relationship between omniscience and partial viewpoints. It is preserved in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit and transmitted with traditional commentaries in Sanskrit and Gujarati within the Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka and related communities.

primary_sources.title: Anuyogadvāra-sūtra (Anuyogadvara-sutta)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to the canonical redaction of the Śvetāmbara Jain community; specific individual authorship is not asserted.
primary_sources.original_text: jāvaṇṇā ya anuyogā, teṇaṃ dvāreṇa pavisanti; bahuvidhā ya anuyogā, teṇaṃ dvāreṇa niggacchanti.
primary_sources.transliteration: jāvaṇṇā ya anuyogā, teṇaṃ dvāreṇa pavisanti; bahuvidhā ya anuyogā, teṇaṃ dvāreṇa niggacchanti.
primary_sources.translation: Various expositions enter by means of this gateway, and many kinds of expositions depart by means of this gateway.
primary_sources.notes: This representative line reflects the central metaphor of the Anuyogadvāra-sūtra: the idea of "gateways" (dvāra) through which different forms of scriptural exposition (anuyoga) are organized. The text classifies narrative, doctrinal, analytical, and other modes of discourse, providing a framework for how teachers structure sermons and scholastic works. It is part of the Śvetāmbara canon and is studied with traditional commentaries that elaborate its technical terminology and its role in hermeneutics.

misconceptions.myth: The Culika-sutras are minor, non-canonical texts that can be ignored in serious study of Jainism.
misconceptions.reality: In the Śvetāmbara tradition, the Culika-sutras are recognized as part of the canonical corpus and play an important role in organizing and interpreting the teachings. They provide key classifications of knowledge and exposition that underlie later Jain philosophy and pedagogy, and are therefore central for understanding how the canon is studied and taught.

misconceptions.myth: The Culika-sutras present entirely new doctrines that differ from the rest of the Jain canon.
misconceptions.reality: The Culika-sutras do not primarily introduce new doctrinal content; instead, they systematize and classify existing teachings. Their focus is on hermeneutics, methods of exposition, and the structure of knowledge. They presuppose the doctrines found in the Aṅgas and other canonical texts and provide tools for understanding and teaching those doctrines more effectively.

misconceptions.myth: Only monastics can benefit from studying the Culika-sutras, and they have no relevance for lay practitioners.
misconceptions.reality: While the Culika-sutras are indeed central in monastic education and advanced scriptural study, their insights into how teachings are organized and communicated can also be valuable for lay students. In many contemporary Śvetāmbara communities, serious lay practitioners and scholars engage with these texts—often through commentaries and guided study—to deepen their understanding of Jain doctrine and its systematic presentation.
